name: Pitcairn Island

pin.note: Approximate centre of Pitcairn Island, near Adamstown (25°04′S 130°06′W)

territory: Pitcairn, Henderson, Ducie and Oeno Islands - a British Overseas Territory (United Kingdom)

creatures.iucn_status: Endangered (uplisted from Vulnerable in 2008; Vulnerable D1+2 proposed in the 2026.1 Red List update, not yet confirmed as final)
creatures.status_note: Endemic to Pitcairn Island, estimated at about 1,568 birds in 2022/23; recent work suggests a stable population but a very small range.

facts.statement: Pitcairn Island is centred at roughly 25.07 degrees south, 130.11 degrees west (25°04′S, 130°06′W) in the South Pacific.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn lies in the isolated south-central Pacific, about 2,170 km southeast of Tahiti.
facts.evidence_note: Opening summary gives the distance and direction from Tahiti.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is the only inhabited island of its territory, and the UNESCO listing places it about 200 km southwest of uninhabited Henderson Island.
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Site description states Pitcairn lies roughly 200 km to the southwest of Henderson.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pitcairn group has four islands (Pitcairn, Henderson, Ducie and Oeno) with about 47 km2 of land in total, of which Henderson accounts for about 86%.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn lies just south of the Tropic of Capricorn and is warm all year; one source gives an average temperature range of 19-24 °C.
facts.evidence_note: Climate line in infobox/section plus territory page note on the Tropic of Capricorn.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Adamstown's climate is classed as tropical rainforest (Köppen Af) with no dry season; February is warmest (mean 23.8 °C) and August coolest (mean 18.5 °C).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Annual rainfall on Pitcairn is about 1,543 mm, spread fairly evenly through the year, with southeast trade winds moderating the climate.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section; the territory article independently gives about 1,540 mm.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pacific Union College Pitcairn Islands Study Center reports average rainfall near 2,000 mm, with 2,170 mm measured on Pitcairn in 1991/92, and monthly mean temperatures from about 24 °C (January) to 19 °C (July).
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Islands Study Center: wetlands and environment
facts.publisher: Pacific Union College Pitcairn Islands Study Center
facts.evidence_note: Climate paragraph of the environment page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Recorded extremes at Pitcairn include a high of 33.3 °C in March, and temperatures have not fallen below 10 °C; tropical cyclones are a hazard mainly from November to May.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is a volcanic island with a rugged cliff-lined coast and no protective coral reefs around it.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The highest point is the Pawala Valley Ridge, given as 346 m above sea level by one source and 347 m by another.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox elevation (346 m); geography article gives 347 m.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is small: about 4.5 km2, roughly 3.5 km long and 1.8 km wide according to one source (others give 5 km2 or 450 ha).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Adamstown is the island's only settlement, and the only landing is a small pier at Bounty Bay, linked to the town by a steep road called the Hill of Difficulty.
facts.evidence_note: Settlement description; the Pitcairn Island article also notes the Bounty Bay pier as sole access.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Within the group Pitcairn is volcanic, Henderson is an uplifted coral island, and Oeno and Ducie are coral atolls.
facts.evidence_note: Geology list of the four islands.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Polynesians settled Pitcairn and Henderson around the 11th century, and contact with other islands such as Mangareva faded by the mid-1400s; both islands were later found uninhabited.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Captain Philip Carteret's crew sighted Pitcairn on 3 July 1767, though his recorded longitude was about 3 degrees off.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Mutineers from HMS Bounty reached Pitcairn on 15 January 1790 and burned the ship on 23 January, settling with 18 Tahitians (6 men, 12 women) and an infant girl.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On 20 September 1793 violence killed most of the remaining English settlers, including Fletcher Christian; John Adams later became the community's leader.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The American sealer Topaz found the settlement in February 1808, and a 1814 visit by two Royal Navy ships counted 46 islanders.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Islanders traditionally date British colony status to 30 November 1838; on 8 June 1856 163 residents moved to Norfolk Island, and some later returned.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is a British Overseas Territory, the only one in the Pacific, under a 2010 constitution; the UK keeps responsibility for defence and foreign affairs.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Local government is led by an elected Island Council that acts as the legislature, with a Mayor customarily heading day-to-day administration and a King's Governor appointed from the UK.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Population is tiny: 35 permanent residents were estimated in 2023, down from a peak of 233 in 1937, mostly through emigration to Australia and New Zealand.
facts.evidence_note: Population section; the Adamstown article also gives 35 for 2023.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Native land animals on Pitcairn are insects and lizards, large numbers of seabirds nest on its steep shores, and humpback whales pass or breed in surrounding waters.
facts.evidence_note: Fauna paragraph; territory article mentions humpbacks breeding.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Of the territory's 20 breeding bird species, 16 breed on Henderson Island, which is also home to the flightless Henderson crake.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Henderson Island has four endemic land birds, ten endemic vascular plant taxa out of about 57 native, and roughly one-third of collected insects and snails are endemic; it is the only known breeding site of the Henderson petrel.
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Species/endemism paragraph of the inscription text.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn's waters hold at least 1,249 species of marine mammals, seabirds and fish, and the reserve includes a coralline alga living 382 m below the surface.
facts.source_title: Pew, National Geographic Applaud Creation of Pitcairn Islands Marine Reserve
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The plant Abutilon pitcairnense, once native to Pitcairn, is now extinct in the wild, and about 16 plant species are thought endemic to Pitcairn.
facts.evidence_note: Flora note; endemic count from the territory article.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO lists three threats on Henderson Island: invasive rats (Polynesian rat) that deplete bird populations, unguarded landings by visitors, and marine plastic debris washing ashore.
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2011 poison-baiting campaign against Pacific rats on Henderson failed: 60-80 survivors out of an estimated 50,000-100,000 rats allowed full recovery.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The UK government announced a marine reserve of about 834,334 km2 around the islands on 18 March 2015, monitored with satellite surveillance against illegal fishing.
facts.source_title: Pew, National Geographic Applaud Creation of Pitcairn Islands Marine Reserve
facts.evidence_note: Size, date and protections; Visit Pitcairn gives ~834,000 km2 and a September 2016 legal designation.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Henderson Island was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988 under natural criteria (vii) and (x).
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pitcairn reed warbler (Acrocephalus vaughani) is found only on Pitcairn Island; it was formally described by Sharpe in 1900 and locals call it the sparrow.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: The IUCN Red List category of the Pitcairn reed warbler has been Endangered since it was raised from Vulnerable in 2008 after surveys showed it was rarer than believed.
facts.evidence_note: Status section; the territory article also notes the 2008 listing.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: The warbler is a habitat generalist, most abundant in stands of introduced rose apple and garden scrub, and avoids pandanus monocultures and bare ground.
facts.evidence_note: Habitat paragraph; the Cambridge paper also reports highest abundance in rose apple.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: A 2022/23 survey estimated about 1,568 Pitcairn reed warblers (95% confidence interval 812-3,237).
facts.source_title: Population status of the endemic Pitcairn Reed Warbler Acrocephalus vaughani on Pitcairn Island, South Pacific
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: Of 49 monitored nests, only four failed to fledge young; productivity was 1.07 fledglings per nest, which the authors judge enough to maintain the population.
facts.source_title: Population status of the endemic Pitcairn Reed Warbler Acrocephalus vaughani on Pitcairn Island, South Pacific
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: The 2024 study's authors recommended downlisting the warbler from Endangered to Vulnerable, and a February 2026 Red List discussion proposed Vulnerable under criteria D1+2; final publication was pending.
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Reed-warbler (Acrocephalus vaughani) - 2026.1 Red List discussion
facts.evidence_note: Proposed status paragraph; Cambridge abstract gives the recommendation.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: Threats to the warbler include a possible arrival of other rat species or cats, past habitat loss, and some soil erosion; it currently coexists with Pacific rats.
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Reed-warbler (Acrocephalus vaughani) - 2026.1 Red List discussion
facts.evidence_note: Threats list in the discussion thread.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: GBIF's backbone resolves Acrocephalus vaughani (Sharpe, 1900) as an accepted species in family Acrocephalidae with usage key 5231321.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler
